metadata.pdf_filename: A comparison of single-cell trajectory inference methods.pdf
metadata.apa_citation: Saelens, W., Cannoodt, R., Todorov, H., & Saeys, Y. (2019). A comparison of single-cell trajectory inference methods. Nature Biotechnology, *37*(5), 547–554. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41587-019-0071-9
metadata.source_file: /mnt/e/work/CytoBridge-agent-main-rag/cytobridge_agent/cbio_agent/literature_db/literature/A comparison of single-cell trajectory inference methods.pdf

content.abstract: This article presents a comparison of single-cell trajectory inference (TI) methods used to model dynamic processes like cell differentiation. It highlights that while early methods required fixed topologies, recent advancements allow for the unbiased inference of complex trajectory structures. The study emphasizes the need for scalable and accurate TI methods to handle growing single-cell datasets and provides a framework for understanding the distinctions between the numerous available tools.

key_objects: Trajectory topologies (linear, bifurcating, tree-shaped, cyclic, disconnected)
key_technical_contributions: A comprehensive comparison framework for existing trajectory inference methods
Classification of TI methods based on their ability to fix or infer trajectory topology
Identification of key distinctions between algorithms regarding required prior information and output topologies
key_scientific_conclusions: TI methods provide an unbiased, transcriptome-wide understanding of dynamic processes like differentiation.
A major distinction between methods is whether they fix the topology algorithmically or infer it from the data.
Recent methods capable of inferring complex topologies (cyclic, disconnected) allow for more unbiased analysis but increase computational complexity.
There is an urgent need for accurate, scalable, and user-friendly TI methods suitable for whole-organism transcriptomic catalogs.

innovation_assessment.reason: The paper addresses a critical bottleneck in the rapidly expanding field of single-cell analysis by systematically reviewing and categorizing the plethora of trajectory inference methods. Establishing a standard for comparison and highlighting the shift from fixed-topology to inferred-topology methods provides significant guidance for the field.

potential_applications: Identification of new cell subsets (e.g., primed cells)
Inference of regulatory interactions responsible for bifurcations
method_strengths: Provides unbiased understanding of dynamic biological processes
Enables objective identification of novel cell subsets
Recent methods support complex topologies (cyclic, disconnected graphs)
Applicable to various single-cell omics data types (transcriptomics, proteomics, epigenomics)
method_limitations: Early methods require prior knowledge or user-defined parameters for topology
Inferring topology increases computational difficulty
Scalability remains a challenge for whole-organism datasets
High variability in algorithm characteristics and outputs makes method selection difficult
analysis.summary: This article presents a comparison of single-cell trajectory inference (TI) methods used to model dynamic processes like cell differentiation. It highlights that while early methods required fixed topologies, recent advancements allow for the unbiased inference of complex trajectory structures. The study emphasizes the need for scalable and accurate TI methods to handle growing single-cell datasets and provides a framework for understanding the distinctions between the numerous available tools.
analysis.title: A comparison of single-cell trajectory inference methods

keywords: Trajectory topologies (linear, bifurcating, tree-shaped, cyclic, disconnected)

metadata.pdf_filename: A semi-supervised Bayesian approach for marker gene trajectory inference from single-cell RNA-seq data.pdf
metadata.apa_citation: Wang, J., Sun, L., Wei, N., Huang, Y., & Zhang, N. (2025). A semi-supervised Bayesian approach for marker gene trajectory inference from single-cell RNA-seq data. Bioinformatics, *41*(9), Article btaf454. https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btaf454
metadata.source_file: /mnt/e/work/CytoBridge-agent-main-rag/cytobridge_agent/cbio_agent/literature_db/literature/A semi-supervised Bayesian approach for marker gene trajectory inference from single-cell RNA-seq data.pdf

content.abstract: This paper presents BayesTraj, a semi-supervised Bayesian framework designed to infer differentiation trajectories from single-cell RNA-seq data. By integrating prior knowledge of lineage topology and marker-gene expression, BayesTraj addresses the limitations of unsupervised methods, such as sensitivity to noise and sparsity. Using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for inference, the method estimates pseudotime and lineage proportions. Evaluations demonstrate that BayesTraj outperforms state-of-the-art methods and enables the quantification of differentiation potential via branch-assignment probabilities.

key_technical_contributions: Development of BayesTraj, a semi-supervised framework that integrates prior knowledge of lineage topology and marker-gene expression.
Modeling cellular differentiation as a probabilistic mixture of latent lineages to capture marker-gene dynamics.
Utilization of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for posterior inference to estimate pseudotime, lineage proportions, and gene activation parameters.
Introduction of methods for quantifying differentiation potential using Shannon entropy based on branch-assignment probabilities.
key_scientific_conclusions: BayesTraj consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in pseudotime inference on both simulated and real datasets.
Incorporating prior knowledge effectively mitigates issues related to technical noise and data sparsity in trajectory inference.
The framework successfully provides per-cell branch-assignment probabilities, aiding in the quantification of differentiation potential.

innovation_assessment.reason: The study addresses critical limitations of existing unsupervised methods (noise and sparsity sensitivity) by proposing a novel semi-supervised Bayesian approach. It demonstrates superior performance over state-of-the-art techniques and introduces new capabilities for probabilistic branch assignment and differentiation potential quantification.

method_strengths: Robustness to technical noise and data sparsity due to semi-supervised nature
Superior performance in pseudotime inference compared to existing methods
Provides probabilistic branch assignments rather than hard assignments
Ability to incorporate prior biological knowledge
method_limitations: Requires prior knowledge of lineage topology and marker genes, which may not be available for all biological systems
Dependency on the quality of the input prior knowledge
analysis.summary: This paper presents BayesTraj, a semi-supervised Bayesian framework designed to infer differentiation trajectories from single-cell RNA-seq data. By integrating prior knowledge of lineage topology and marker-gene expression, BayesTraj addresses the limitations of unsupervised methods, such as sensitivity to noise and sparsity. Using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for inference, the method estimates pseudotime and lineage proportions. Evaluations demonstrate that BayesTraj outperforms state-of-the-art methods and enables the quantification of differentiation potential via branch-assignment probabilities.
analysis.title: A semi-supervised Bayesian approach for marker gene trajectory inference from single-cell RNA-seq data

It highlights how these techniques overcome the limitations of traditional bulk sequencing by revealing cellular heterogeneity, dynamic states, and rare populations. The paper discusses methodological principles, strengths, limitations, and presents case studies across fields like developmental biology, cancer, and precision medicine, emphasizing the power of integrating multiple omics layers.

Integration of multimodal omics data within a single cell
Characterization of diverse cell types, dynamic cellular states, and rare cell populations

Multimodal omics integration provides a holistic view of cellular processes and regulatory networks.
These technologies significantly enhance the understanding of cellular systems in development and disease contexts.

content.abstract: This study assesses GPT-4's ability to annotate cell types in single-cell RNA-seq analysis. The authors developed the GPTCelltype R package and demonstrated that GPT-4 generates annotations showing strong concordance with manual annotations across diverse datasets. This approach significantly reduces the labor and expertise required for cell type annotation, offering a cost-effective and automated solution.

key_methods: Benchmarking against GPT-3.5, SingleR, ScType, and CellMarker2.0

Development of GPTCelltype, an R software package for automated cell type annotation
Establishment of a pipeline that integrates LLMs into scRNA-seq analysis without requiring reference datasets
key_scientific_conclusions: GPT-4 generates cell type annotations with strong concordance to manual annotations across hundreds of tissues and cell types
LLM-based annotation significantly reduces the effort and expertise required for scRNA-seq analysis
GPT-4 offers a cost-efficient and broadly applicable solution compared to existing automated methods

innovation_assessment.reason: The study pioneers the application of Large Language Models (GPT-4) to the critical bottleneck of cell type annotation in single-cell analysis. It replaces labor-intensive manual processes with an automated, accurate, and reference-free approach, validated across extensive datasets.

content.abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive benchmarking study for atlas-level data integration in single-cell genomics. Addressing the limitations of previous studies that focused on simple batch effects, the authors evaluate integration methods on complex, nonlinear, and nested batch effects typical of reference atlas initiatives. The study aims to provide an unbiased guide for method selection, comparing various outputs like joint embeddings and corrected feature matrices.

key_objects: reference atlas initiatives (e.g., Human Cell Atlas)
key_technical_contributions: A comprehensive benchmarking framework specifically designed for atlas-level data integration
Evaluation of methods on complex, nonlinear, and nested batch effects
Comparison of different integration output types (corrected features vs. joint embeddings)
key_scientific_conclusions: Previous benchmarking studies focused on simple integration tasks and favored linear methods like Harmony or ComBat
Atlas-level data requires methods capable of handling complex, nonlinear, nested batch effects
Objective metrics are essential to replace subjective visual evaluations for method selection

innovation_assessment.reason: The study addresses a critical gap in the field by providing the first comprehensive benchmark for atlas-level integration, moving beyond simple batch correction to handle the complexity of modern single-cell datasets.

potential_applications: Guiding method selection for single-cell data analysis pipelines
Construction of large-scale reference cell atlases
Improving the accuracy of downstream analyses such as clustering and cell type annotation
method_strengths: Objective evaluation metrics
Focus on complex, real-world data scenarios (atlas-level)
Broad coverage of existing integration methods (49 methods)

metadata.source_file: /mnt/e/work/CytoBridge-agent-main-rag/cytobridge_agent/cbio_agent/literature_db/literature/CellRank 2 unified fate mapping in multiview single-cell data.pdf

content.abstract: CellRank 2 presents a versatile and scalable framework for unified fate mapping using multiview single-cell data, addressing the limitations of existing single-modality methods. By decomposing trajectory inference into modality-specific transition modeling and modality-agnostic analysis, it handles millions of cells and integrates diverse inputs like RNA velocity, experimental time points, and metabolic labeling. The framework successfully identified differentiation dynamics in hematopoiesis, endoderm development, and intestinal organoids.

key_technical_contributions: Developed CellRank 2, a unified and scalable framework for analyzing multiview single-cell data
Decomposed trajectory inference into modality-specific transition modeling and modality-agnostic TI
Enabled the combination of transitions within and across experimental time points
Introduced methods to estimate cell-specific transcription and degradation rates from metabolic-labeling data
Achieved scalability to process datasets containing millions of cells
key_scientific_conclusions: CellRank 2 consistently recovers terminal states and fate probabilities across different data modalities
The framework successfully identified genes promoting medullary thymic epithelial cell formation in pharyngeal endoderm development
Applied to intestinal organoids, the method delineated differentiation trajectories and pinpointed regulatory strategies
The modular approach overcomes limitations of single-modality methods like WOT and Dynamo

innovation_assessment.reason: The paper introduces a novel, modular framework that unifies multiple data modalities (RNA velocity, experimental time points, metabolic labeling) for trajectory inference, overcoming the scalability and single-modality limitations of existing state-of-the-art methods.

method_strengths: Unified framework for multiview data integration
High scalability to millions of cells
Modular architecture allowing flexibility
Ability to combine experimental time points with state transitions
Applicability to diverse biological systems
method_limitations: Performance relies on the quality and compatibility of input data modalities
Complexity of integrating diverse data views may require parameter tuning
Dependence on accurate modality-specific transition models
analysis.summary: CellRank 2 presents a versatile and scalable framework for unified fate mapping using multiview single-cell data, addressing the limitations of existing single-modality methods. metadata.apa_citation: Ling, Y., Zhang, P., Zhang, Z., & Zhou, P. (2025). CellStream: Dynamical optimal transport informed embeddings for reconstructing cellular trajectories from snapshots data. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.13786
metadata.source_file: /mnt/e/work/CytoBridge-agent-main-rag/cytobridge_agent/cbio_agent/literature_db/literature/CellStream Dynamical Optimal Transport Informed Embeddings for Reconstructing Cellular Trajectories from Snapshots Data.pdf

content.abstract: CellStream is a deep learning framework designed to reconstruct continuous cellular trajectories from static scRNA-seq snapshots. By integrating an autoencoder with unbalanced dynamical optimal transport, it jointly learns embeddings and cellular dynamics, overcoming the limitation of separating trajectory inference from embedding construction. Experiments demonstrate that CellStream outperforms state-of-the-art methods in temporal coherence and noise robustness across simulated and real datasets, including spatial transcriptomics.

key_technical_contributions: Proposed CellStream, a novel framework integrating autoencoder with unbalanced dynamical optimal transport
Joint learning of low-dimensional embeddings and cellular dynamics from snapshot data
Development of dynamics-informed embeddings that preserve temporal structure
key_scientific_conclusions: CellStream effectively reconstructs continuous cellular trajectories from discrete, static snapshots
The method demonstrates superior performance over state-of-the-art methods in temporal coherence and noise reduction
Validated effectiveness on both simulated datasets and real scRNA-seq data, including spatial transcriptomics

innovation_assessment.reason: The paper addresses a critical gap by jointly learning embeddings and dynamics, unlike existing methods that treat them separately. The integration of unbalanced dynamical optimal transport with autoencoders offers a novel solution to the snapshot problem in scRNA-seq.

method_strengths: Joint optimization of embedding and dynamics
Robustness to technical noise
High consistency with underlying data manifold
Enhanced temporal coherence

content.abstract: CFM-GP introduces a unified conditional flow matching framework to predict gene perturbation effects across cell types using a single model. By learning a continuous transformation conditioned on cell type, it overcomes the scalability limitations of cell type-specific models. Evaluated on five datasets, CFM-GP outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in accuracy and recovers key biological pathways, demonstrating its potential for scalable functional genomics.

key_technical_contributions: Proposed CFM-GP, a unified model for gene perturbation prediction across cell types
Applied flow matching objective to model perturbation dynamics in a scalable manner
Eliminated the need for cell type-specific training models by conditioning on cell type
key_scientific_conclusions: CFM-GP consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in R squared scores and Spearman rank correlations
The model accurately captures the relative ordering of gene expression changes
Predictions recover key biological pathways activated by perturbations, confirming biological fidelity
The method establishes a scalable solution for cross-cell type perturbation prediction

innovation_assessment.reason: The paper introduces a novel cell type-agnostic approach using Conditional Flow Matching, addressing the critical scalability limitation of existing methods that require separate models for each cell type. This represents a significant methodological advancement in modeling perturbation dynamics.

method_strengths: Scalability through a single unified model
High prediction accuracy compared to baselines
Ability to generalize across diverse cell types and perturbations
Biological fidelity in recovering activated pathways
method_limitations: Performance likely depends on the diversity and quality of the training data
Modeling continuous transformations may be complex for highly distinct cellular contexts

metadata.apa_citation: Wang, N., He, Y., Ray, E. et al. CiCLoDS: Joint cell clustering and gene selection for single-cell spatial transcriptomics. Sci Rep 16, 5356 (2026). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-39168-1
metadata.source_file: /mnt/e/work/CytoBridge-agent-main-rag/cytobridge_agent/cbio_agent/literature_db/literature/CiCLoDS Joint cell clustering and gene selection for single-cell spatial transcriptomics.pdf

content.abstract: CiCLoDS is an unsupervised framework for spatial transcriptomics that jointly optimizes cell clustering and gene selection under a strict gene budget. Utilizing sine–cosine positional encodings, it integrates spatial information to identify critical low-dimensional subspaces. Benchmarked on MERFISH, Xenium, and Visium datasets, CiCLoDS outperforms sequential methods like PCA and BayesCafe in accuracy (ARI) and neighborhood preservation. It offers a lightweight, efficient solution that produces assay-ready gene panels and enhances the performance of existing tools like BayesSpace through synergistic initialization.

key_methods: Joint optimization of clustering and feature selection
Sine–cosine positional encodings for spatial information
Benchmarking against PCA, geneBasis, and BayesSpace
key_technical_contributions: Developed CiCLoDS, a framework that jointly optimizes clustering and feature selection under a strict user-defined gene budget.
Introduced the use of sine–cosine positional encodings to incorporate spatial side information into the clustering process.
Demonstrated a synergistic utility where CiCLoDS initializes BayesSpace to resolve local minima issues and improve performance.
key_scientific_conclusions: Joint optimization of clustering and feature selection outperforms traditional sequential dimensionality reduction methods like PCA.
CiCLoDS achieves higher Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) scores (up to +0.36 improvement) and better preservation of neighborhood structure.
The method demonstrates robust generalization across diverse datasets (mouse liver, human colon, human DLPFC) and platforms.
The lightweight objective function converges in minutes on commodity CPUs, making it computationally efficient.

innovation_assessment.reason: The paper addresses a critical bottleneck in spatial transcriptomics by jointly optimizing clustering and feature selection under a strict gene budget, a departure from standard sequential pipelines. The integration of spatial encodings and the demonstrated synergistic utility with existing tools like BayesSpace represent significant methodological advancements.

potential_applications: Design of targeted gene panels for spatial transcriptomic assays
Identification of cellular neighborhoods and tissue architecture
Preprocessing and initialization for downstream spatial analysis tools
method_strengths: Joint optimization ensures the selected gene subset is directly aligned with clustering results.
Computational efficiency (converges in minutes on CPUs).
Robust generalization across different spatial transcriptomics platforms.
Interpretable output with an explicit, compact feature subset.
Synergistic compatibility with other analysis methods like BayesSpace.
method_limitations: Relies on a user-defined gene budget, which requires prior knowledge or trial-and-error to optimize.
Performance is benchmarked primarily on specific datasets; behavior on extremely sparse or low-quality data needs further validation.

content.abstract: This paper presents the Compositional Perturbation Autoencoder (CPA), a deep learning model designed to predict single-cell responses to drug and genetic perturbations. By combining the interpretability of linear models with the flexibility of deep learning, CPA learns transcriptional responses across different cell types, doses, and combinations. The model accurately predicts unseen perturbations and genetic interactions, facilitating efficient in-silico experimental design.

Learning easy-to-interpret embeddings for drugs and cell types
Prediction of unseen dosages and drug combinations
In-silico generation of missing combinatorial interactions
key_scientific_conclusions: CPA accurately models single-cell perturbations across compounds, dosages, species, and time
The model successfully predicts combinatorial genetic interactions
It enables the in-silico generation of a vast majority (97.6%) of missing experimental combinations

innovation_assessment.reason: The paper addresses the critical bottleneck of experimentally infeasible combinatorial perturbation spaces by proposing a novel architecture that balances interpretability with predictive power, enabling predictions for unseen drug combinations and genetic interactions at single-cell resolution.

potential_applications: Optimizing experimental design via in-silico predictions
method_strengths: Interpretability of drug and cell type embeddings
Ability to model combinatorial perturbations
Prediction of unseen dosages and combinations
High throughput capability

content.abstract: This paper introduces PINNACLE, a geometric deep learning approach designed to generate context-aware protein representations by leveraging a multiorgan single-cell atlas. PINNACLE learns from contextualized protein interaction networks to produce 394,760 protein representations across 156 cell types and 24 tissues. The model's embedding space captures cellular and tissue organization, enabling zero-shot retrieval of tissue hierarchies. It demonstrates superior performance over state-of-the-art models in identifying therapeutic targets for rheumatoid arthritis and inflammatory bowel diseases, highlighting the importance of biological context in protein modeling.

content.abstract: This paper introduces GeneTrajectory, a novel method utilizing optimal transport metrics to infer gene trajectories from single-cell RNA sequencing data. Unlike traditional cell trajectory inference, GeneTrajectory focuses on gene distributions across a cell-cell graph to define gene pseudotemporal order. This approach effectively deconvolves concurrent biological processes and identifies gene programs in complex scenarios like myeloid maturation and hair follicle differentiation, offering superior resolution compared to existing cell-based methods.

content.abstract: This paper presents a dynamical modeling approach to generalize the concept of RNA velocity, addressing the limitations of the original steady-state model. By modeling the relationship between unspliced and spliced mRNA without assuming steady-state equilibrium, the method enables the inference of transcriptional dynamics in transient cell states. This advancement allows for predictive trajectory inference from standard scRNA-seq data, facilitating a deeper understanding of cellular differentiation and lineage choice.

content.abstract: This paper presents MultiVeloVAE, a probabilistic framework designed to infer RNA velocity from multi-lineage, multi-sample, and multi-omic single-cell data. It integrates gene expression and chromatin accessibility on a shared time scale and enables statistical testing of differential dynamics. Validated on human embryoid bodies and differentiating macrophages, the method offers new insights into the regulatory dynamics of cell differentiation.

key_technical_contributions: Developed MultiVeloVAE for multi-sample RNA velocity inference
Integrated gene expression and chromatin accessibility on a shared time scale
Enabled statistical testing of velocity parameters for identifying differential dynamics
Supported analysis of multi-lineage, multi-sample, and multi-omic datasets
key_scientific_conclusions: MultiVeloVAE successfully infers differential dynamics from complex single-cell datasets
The method provides novel insights into chromatin accessibility and gene expression dynamics during development
It overcomes limitations of previous RNA velocity methods by supporting multi-sample and multi-omic integration

innovation_assessment.reason: The paper introduces a comprehensive framework that addresses significant gaps in current RNA velocity inference (multi-lineage, multi-sample, multi-omic support) and introduces statistical testing for differential dynamics, representing a substantial methodological advancement.

method_strengths: Supports multi-lineage, multi-sample, and multi-omic data integration
Models expression and accessibility on a shared time scale
Enables statistical testing of velocity parameters
Handles datasets with partially overlapping modalities
method_limitations: Requires multi-omic data input which can be expensive to generate
Computational complexity may be higher than standard velocity methods
analysis.summary: This paper presents MultiVeloVAE, a probabilistic framework designed to infer RNA velocity from multi-lineage, multi-sample, and multi-omic single-cell data. It integrates gene expression and chromatin accessibility on a shared time scale and enables statistical testing of differential dynamics. Validated on human embryoid bodies and differentiating macrophages, the method offers new insights into the regulatory dynamics of cell differentiation.

metadata.title: Kinetic Optimal Transport (OTIKIN) -- Part 1 Second-Order Discrepancies Between Probability Measures
metadata.pdf_filename: Kinetic Optimal Transport (OTIKIN) -- Part 1 Second-Order Discrepancies Between Probability Measures.pdf
metadata.apa_citation: Brigati, G., Maas, J., & Quattrocchi, F. (2025). Kinetic optimal transport (OTIKIN) – Part 1: Second-order discrepancies between probability measures. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.15665
metadata.source_file: /mnt/e/work/CytoBridge-agent-main-rag/cytobridge_agent/cbio_agent/literature_db/literature/Kinetic Optimal Transport (OTIKIN) -- Part 1 Second-Order Discrepancies Between Probability Measures.pdf

content.abstract: This paper introduces OTIKIN, a framework for describing time-evolving interacting particle systems via mass transport. It defines a new second-order discrepancy d between probability measures in phase space, optimizing minimal acceleration cost. The authors prove the existence of optimal maps, establish the equivalence of static and dynamic formulations via Vlasov equations, and develop a differential calculus for the induced geometry.

key_technical_contributions: Introduction of a novel second-order discrepancy d between probability distributions in position and velocity states.
Construction of the discrepancy d via optimization over transport plans (based on minimal acceleration) and time horizon.
Proof of existence of optimal transport plans and maps for the proposed discrepancy.
Establishment of equivalence between static and dynamical formulations using an original proof involving Galilean regularization.
Development of a first-order differential calculus in the geometry induced by the new discrepancy.
key_scientific_conclusions: The new discrepancy d is well-defined and possesses optimal transport plans and maps.
Static and dynamical formulations of d are equivalent.
Solutions to Vlasov's equations can be identified with curves of measures satisfying d-absolute continuity.
An explicit formula for the d-derivative of such curves has been derived.
The framework successfully bridges kinetic theory and optimal transport.

innovation_assessment.reason: The paper introduces a fundamental theoretical extension of Optimal Transport to kinetic theory by defining a new second-order discrepancy. It creates original mathematical tools (Galilean regularization, kinetic Monge-Mather shortening) to solve open problems regarding the equivalence of static and dynamic formulations in this context.

method_strengths: Strong theoretical foundation with rigorous proofs.
Generalizes the classical Wasserstein distance to a second-order context involving velocity.
Provides a dynamic interpretation linked to physical principles (acceleration, Vlasov equations).
Establishes a differential calculus allowing for further analytical development.
method_limitations: Highly theoretical and mathematical, requiring advanced knowledge of optimal transport and PDEs.
Computational implementation is not discussed in this part, potentially posing challenges due to the complexity of the optimization.
Currently limited to the mesoscopic level description.
analysis.summary: This paper introduces OTIKIN, a framework for describing time-evolving interacting particle systems via mass transport. It defines a new second-order discrepancy d between probability measures in phase space, optimizing minimal acceleration cost. The authors prove the existence of optimal maps, establish the equivalence of static and dynamic formulations via Vlasov equations, and develop a differential calculus for the induced geometry.
analysis.title: Kinetic Optimal Transport (OTIKIN) -- Part 1 Second-Order Discrepancies Between Probability Measures

content.abstract: This paper presents CellOT, a framework utilizing neural optimal transport to predict single-cell perturbation responses by mapping unpaired distributions. Addressing the limitation of destructive measurements, CellOT outperforms existing methods in drug response prediction and demonstrates robust generalization to unseen patients and cross-species contexts, offering a powerful tool for understanding heterogeneous cellular reactions.

Leveraged input convex neural architectures to learn individual cell responses without requiring paired measurements
Demonstrated superior performance over existing methods in predicting drug responses
key_scientific_conclusions: CellOT outperforms current methods in predicting single-cell drug responses across different profiling technologies
The framework generalizes well to unseen patient data (lupus, glioblastoma) and cross-species settings
Successfully modeled hematopoietic developmental trajectories, proving its utility beyond chemical perturbations

innovation_assessment.reason: The paper addresses a fundamental challenge in single-cell biology (unpaired data due to destructive measurements) by novelly applying neural optimal transport. The method demonstrates superior performance and broad generalization capabilities, published in a top-tier journal (Nature Methods).

method_strengths: Solves the unpaired distribution problem inherent to single-cell measurements
Superior predictive performance compared to existing methods
Strong generalization to unseen patients and different species
Versatile application to various data types (scRNA-seq, protein imaging)
method_limitations: Requires sufficient sample size to accurately estimate cell distributions
Assumes the existence of a transport map between control and perturbed distributions

metadata.source_file: /mnt/e/work/CytoBridge-agent-main-rag/cytobridge_agent/cbio_agent/literature_db/literature/Learning stochastic dynamics from snapshots through regularized unbalanced optimal transport.pdf

content.abstract: This paper presents a deep learning approach to solve Regularized Unbalanced Optimal Transport (RUOT) for reconstructing stochastic dynamics from sparsely sampled snapshots. The method uniquely infers growth and transition patterns without prior knowledge of birth/death processes. Validated on synthetic gene networks and scRNA-seq data, it demonstrates superior accuracy in eliminating false transitions and reconstructing developmental landscapes.

key_technical_contributions: A novel deep learning approach for solving Regularized Unbalanced Optimal Transport (RUOT)
Inference of continuous unbalanced stochastic dynamics directly from observed snapshots
Modeling dynamics without requiring prior knowledge of growth and death processes
Theoretical exploration of the connection between RUOT and the Schrödinger bridge problem
key_scientific_conclusions: The proposed method accurately identifies growth and transition patterns in synthetic and biological data
It effectively eliminates false transitions compared to existing methods
The approach successfully constructs the Waddington developmental landscape for blood development
Unbalanced dynamics can be learned directly from data without additional information

innovation_assessment.reason: The paper introduces a novel deep learning framework for RUOT that addresses the critical challenge of unbalanced mass (growth/death) in snapshot data, removing the need for prior biological assumptions often required by existing methods.

potential_applications: Interpolating paths between arbitrary high-dimensional distributions
method_strengths: Does not require prior knowledge of growth and death processes
Handles unbalanced optimal transport problems effectively
Eliminates false transitions in dynamical inference
Applicable to high-dimensional data
method_limitations: Theoretical complexity in connecting RUOT with the Schrödinger bridge problem
Potential challenges in solving the RUOT formulation accurately
analysis.summary: This paper presents a deep learning approach to solve Regularized Unbalanced Optimal Transport (RUOT) for reconstructing stochastic dynamics from sparsely sampled snapshots. The method uniquely infers growth and transition patterns without prior knowledge of birth/death processes. Validated on synthetic gene networks and scRNA-seq data, it demonstrates superior accuracy in eliminating false transitions and reconstructing developmental landscapes.

content.abstract: This review systematically surveys the landscape of spatial transcriptomics (ST), summarizing 594 analysis tools and 77 technologies. It outlines a complete analytical workflow covering preprocessing, pattern identification, and multi-omics integration, while highlighting platform-dependent considerations. A key contribution is the development of SpatialToolDB, a curated database designed to facilitate tool selection and method comparison, thereby supporting biomedical discoveries in tissue architecture and cellular interactions.

Systematic categorization of 594 ST analysis tools and 77 ST technologies
Establishment of a complete ST analytical workflow framework
Identification of platform-dependent considerations for method selection
key_scientific_conclusions: ST technologies provide crucial spatial context for understanding tissue microenvironments
Analytical methods must be selected based on platform-specific resolution and detection efficiency
ST data analysis enables discovery of spatial heterogeneity and context-dependent cellular interactions
Rapid advancement in the field necessitates systematic resources for tool comparison

innovation_assessment.reason: The study provides a massive systematic review of 594 tools and introduces SpatialToolDB, a valuable curated database resource that addresses the challenge of tool selection in a rapidly evolving field.

potential_applications: Selection of appropriate tools for spatial transcriptomics data analysis
Biomedical research on tissue architecture and disease microenvironment
Development of new algorithms for spatial data processing

metadata.source_file: /mnt/e/work/CytoBridge-agent-main-rag/cytobridge_agent/cbio_agent/literature_db/literature/Mapping cells through time and space with moscot.pdf

content.abstract: This paper presents moscot, a scalable framework for multi-omics single-cell optimal transport that overcomes limitations in scalability and multimodality. The authors demonstrate its ability to reconstruct developmental trajectories of 1.7 million mouse embryo cells, align spatial transcriptomic sections, and uncover spatiotemporal dynamics. Additionally, moscot resolved pancreatic lineage relationships and experimentally validated NEUROD2 as a regulator of epsilon progenitor cells, providing a robust tool for single-cell genomics.

key_technical_contributions: Development of moscot, a scalable framework for multi-omics single-cell optimal transport
Introduction of moscot.spatiotemporal for joint spatiotemporal analysis
Capability to process 1.7 million cells across 20 time points
Integration of paired gene expression and chromatin accessibility data
key_scientific_conclusions: Moscot successfully reconstructs developmental trajectories at scale.
It enables the alignment of spatial sections and enrichment of spatial data with multimodal information.
The framework uncovers spatiotemporal dynamics of mouse embryogenesis.
Resolved endocrine-lineage relationships in pancreas development, identifying NEUROD2 as a regulator for epsilon progenitor cells.

innovation_assessment.reason: Addresses critical scalability and multimodality limitations of existing Optimal Transport methods in single-cell genomics. The ability to handle 1.7 million cells and integrate spatiotemporal data represents a significant methodological advancement.

method_strengths: High scalability (millions of cells)
Multimodality support
Spatiotemporal integration
Open-source availability
Validated by experimental data
method_limitations: Relies on the quality and coverage of input single-cell and spatial data

metadata.source_file: /mnt/e/work/CytoBridge-agent-main-rag/cytobridge_agent/cbio_agent/literature_db/literature/Microenvironment-aware transcriptome reconstruction in spatial transcriptomics.pdf

content.abstract: This paper presents Emerge, a novel framework for reconstructing transcriptome-scale expression in imaging-based spatial transcriptomics. By employing a type-constrained optimal transport formulation, Emerge integrates intrinsic transcriptional manifolds from scRNA-seq with extrinsic spatial niche organization. Tested on fourteen MERFISH and Xenium datasets, the method outperforms existing approaches in accuracy and spatial coherence, successfully revealing microenvironment-stratified cell states and within-type heterogeneity.

Integration of scRNA-seq and imaging-based spatial data
key_technical_contributions: Development of the Emerge framework for transcriptome reconstruction
Introduction of a type-constrained optimal transport algorithm to incorporate spatial microenvironment information
A novel approach to capture within-type heterogeneity driven by the microenvironment, overcoming limitations of shared-gene alignment methods
key_scientific_conclusions: Emerge improves prediction accuracy and spatial coherence of gene expression in spatial transcriptomics
The method successfully recovers within-type heterogeneity that existing methods fail to capture
Reconstructed transcriptomes reveal microenvironment-stratified cell states in neural and tumor tissues

innovation_assessment.reason: The paper addresses a critical limitation of imaging-based spatial transcriptomics (limited gene panels) by proposing a novel optimal transport framework that explicitly models spatial microenvironments. This approach moves beyond standard alignment techniques to capture subtle biological variations, representing a significant methodological advancement.

potential_applications: Enhancement of imaging-based spatial transcriptomics data (MERFISH, Xenium)
Discovery of novel cell states and spatial domains in complex tissues (e.g., tumors, brain)
Spatially resolved cell-type annotation and heterogeneity analysis

High prediction accuracy across diverse datasets
Recovers transcriptome-wide expression from limited gene panels
Demonstrated robustness across fourteen different datasets
method_limitations: Dependence on the availability and quality of matched scRNA-seq reference data

Potential bias if the spatial niche organization is not well-defined in the reference data

metadata.source_file: /mnt/e/work/CytoBridge-agent-main-rag/cytobridge_agent/cbio_agent/literature_db/literature/Multi-omics single-cell data integration and regulatory inference with graph-linked embedding.pdf

content.abstract: This paper presents CellRank 2, a versatile and scalable framework for unified fate mapping using multiview single-cell data. It addresses the limitations of existing trajectory inference methods by decomposing the process into modality-specific transition modeling and modality-agnostic inference. Validated on human hematopoiesis and endodermal development, the framework integrates RNA velocity, experimental time points, and metabolic labeling to accurately recover terminal states and regulatory mechanisms in systems previously inaccessible to standard methods.

key_technical_contributions: Development of CellRank 2, a unified framework for multiview single-cell data analysis
Decomposition of trajectory inference into modality-specific and modality-agnostic components
Scalability to datasets comprising millions of cells
Integration of experimental time points with transition modeling
Method to estimate cell-specific transcription and degradation rates from metabolic-labeling data
key_scientific_conclusions: CellRank 2 consistently recovers terminal states and fate probabilities across diverse data modalities
Successful application to human hematopoiesis where previous RNA velocity models failed
Identification of genes promoting medullary thymic epithelial cell formation
Delineation of differentiation trajectories in intestinal organoid systems

innovation_assessment.reason: The paper introduces a significant extension to a widely used tool (CellRank), solving the critical problem of integrating heterogeneous data modalities (velocity, time, metabolic labeling) into a single scalable framework, overcoming limitations of specialized single-modality methods.

method_strengths: Unified analysis of multiple data modalities
High scalability (millions of cells)
Modular architecture allowing flexibility
Ability to combine experimental time points with state transitions
Robustness in complex biological systems like adult hematopoiesis
method_limitations: Performance depends on the quality and compatibility of input modalities
Potential computational complexity with very large graphs
analysis.summary: This paper presents CellRank 2, a versatile and scalable framework for unified fate mapping using multiview single-cell data. It addresses the limitations of existing trajectory inference methods by decomposing the process into modality-specific transition modeling and modality-agnostic inference. Validated on human hematopoiesis and endodermal development, the framework integrates RNA velocity, experimental time points, and metabolic labeling to accurately recover terminal states and regulatory mechanisms in systems previously inaccessible to standard methods.

metadata.source_file: /mnt/e/work/CytoBridge-agent-main-rag/cytobridge_agent/cbio_agent/literature_db/literature/NicheNet modeling intercellular communication by linking ligands to target genes.pdf

content.abstract: NicheNet is a computational method designed to model intercellular communication by linking ligands to target genes. Unlike existing tools that focus solely on ligand-receptor interactions, NicheNet integrates prior knowledge of signaling and gene regulatory networks to predict the regulatory effects of sender-cell ligands on receiver-cell gene expression. Validated on tumor and immune microenvironment data, it enables a functional understanding of cell-cell interactions.

key_methods: Integration of prior knowledge on signaling and gene regulatory networks
key_technical_contributions: Development of NicheNet, a method to predict ligand-target links between interacting cells
Construction of a prior model integrating ligand-to-target signaling paths beyond simple ligand-receptor interactions
Incorporation of intracellular signaling into intercellular communication modeling
key_scientific_conclusions: NicheNet can infer active ligands and their gene regulatory effects on interacting cells
Functional understanding of cell-cell communication requires linking ligands to target gene expression, not just ligand-receptor binding
The method is applicable to both bulk and single-cell expression data

innovation_assessment.reason: NicheNet addresses a critical gap in the field by moving beyond ligand-receptor interaction identification to predicting the functional downstream effects on target genes, integrating prior knowledge of intracellular signaling pathways.

method_strengths: Combines expression data with prior biological knowledge
Predicts functional gene regulatory effects rather than just interactions
Applicable to both bulk and single-cell data
Incorporates intracellular signaling mechanisms
method_limitations: Dependence on the quality and completeness of prior knowledge databases
Currently focused on human and mouse gene expression data
Complexity of model interpretation due to integration of multiple network layers
analysis.summary: NicheNet is a computational method designed to model intercellular communication by linking ligands to target genes. Unlike existing tools that focus solely on ligand-receptor interactions, NicheNet integrates prior knowledge of signaling and gene regulatory networks to predict the regulatory effects of sender-cell ligands on receiver-cell gene expression. Validated on tumor and immune microenvironment data, it enables a functional understanding of cell-cell interactions.

metadata.apa_citation: Chen, Y., Georgiou, T. T., & Pavon, M. (2016). On the relation between optimal transport and Schrödinger bridges: A stochastic control viewpoint. Journal of Optimization Theory and Applications, *169*(2), 671–691. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10957-015-0803-z
metadata.source_file: /mnt/e/work/CytoBridge-agent-main-rag/cytobridge_agent/cbio_agent/literature_db/literature/On the Relation Between Optimal Transport and Schrödinger Bridges A Stochastic Control Viewpoint.pdf

content.abstract: This paper investigates the relationship between Optimal Mass Transport (OMT) and the Schrödinger Bridge Problem (SBP) from a stochastic control viewpoint. It derives a new fluid dynamic formulation for SBP, showing that the two problems differ by a Fisher information functional, thereby solving a question by Eric Carlen. The work generalizes OMT to 'optimal transport with prior' and provides explicit solutions for Gaussian cases using Riccati equations.

key_technical_contributions: New fluid dynamic version of the Schrödinger bridge problem
Establishment of a connection between SB and OT without zero-noise limits
Identification of Fisher information functional as the difference between the two variational problems
Generalization of optimal mass transport (optimal transport with prior)
Explicit computational theory for Gaussian case based on Riccati equations
key_scientific_conclusions: The Schrödinger bridge problem establishes a connection with optimal transport without requiring zero-noise limits.
The two variational problems differ by a Fisher information functional.
Optimal mass transport emerges as the zero-noise limit of Schrödinger bridges.
The fluid dynamic approach highlights time symmetry and connections to stochastic control.

innovation_assessment.reason: The paper provides a novel stochastic control perspective linking two major fields, solves a specific open question posed by Eric Carlen, and introduces a new fluid dynamic formulation for Schrödinger bridges.

method_strengths: Unified theoretical framework
New insights without limiting arguments
Explicit solutions for Gaussian cases
Rigorous mathematical derivation
method_limitations: Explicit computational theory is limited to the Gaussian case
General non-Gaussian cases may require complex numerical methods

metadata.title: Optimal Entropy-Transport problems and a new Hellinger–Kantorovich distance between positive measures
metadata.pdf_filename: Optimal Entropy-Transport problems and a new Hellinger–Kantorovich distance between positive measures.pdf
metadata.apa_citation: Liero, M., Mielke, A., & Savaré, G. (2018). Optimal entropy-transport problems and a new Hellinger–Kantorovich distance between positive measures. Inventiones Mathematicae, *211*(3), 969–1117. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00222-017-0759-8
metadata.source_file: /mnt/e/work/CytoBridge-agent-main-rag/cytobridge_agent/cbio_agent/literature_db/literature/Optimal Entropy-Transport problems and a new Hellinger–Kantorovich distance between positive measures.pdf

content.abstract: This paper develops a comprehensive theory for Optimal Entropy-Transport problems, relaxing the strict marginal constraints of classical Optimal Transport to handle measures with different total masses. By minimizing a linear transport functional combined with convex entropy functionals, the authors introduce the novel Hellinger–Kantorovich distance. This new metric effectively bridges the gap between Hellinger–Kakutani and Kantorovich–Wasserstein distances, offering new geometric insights for comparing positive measures.

key_technical_contributions: Development of a full theory for Optimal Entropy-Transport problems in general topological spaces
Relaxation of marginal constraints in Optimal Transport by adding convex entropy functionals
Introduction of the new Hellinger–Kantorovich distance between measures
Establishment of a connection between Logarithmic Entropy-Transport and the Hellinger–Kantorovich distance
Analysis of geodesic properties of the new distance metric
key_scientific_conclusions: The new formulation allows for the comparison of measures with different total masses, overcoming a limitation of classical Optimal Transport
The Hellinger–Kantorovich distance serves as a geometric bridge between the Hellinger–Kakutani and Kantorovich–Wasserstein distances
The Entropy-Transport problem provides a robust framework for quantifying deviations in marginal constraints

innovation_assessment.reason: Published in a top-tier mathematics journal (Inventiones mathematicae), the paper introduces a fundamental theoretical advancement by relaxing strict marginal constraints in Optimal Transport and defining a novel metric (Hellinger–Kantorovich) that unifies existing distance concepts.

potential_applications: Image processing and computer vision (e.g., image registration with varying intensities)
Machine learning (comparison of probability distributions with different masses)
Theoretical physics (models involving mass diffusion or creation/destruction)
method_strengths: Generalizes classical Optimal Transport to handle measures with unequal total mass
Provides a rigorous mathematical foundation including existence results and duality
Offers a clear geometric interpretation via the new distance metric
method_limitations: Highly theoretical and abstract, requiring advanced mathematical background
Computational implementation for high-dimensional data may be challenging (not explicitly discussed but implied by complexity)
Focuses primarily on static measures rather than dynamic evolution in this specific text
analysis.summary: This paper develops a comprehensive theory for Optimal Entropy-Transport problems, relaxing the strict marginal constraints of classical Optimal Transport to handle measures with different total masses. By minimizing a linear transport functional combined with convex entropy functionals, the authors introduce the novel Hellinger–Kantorovich distance. This new metric effectively bridges the gap between Hellinger–Kakutani and Kantorovich–Wasserstein distances, offering new geometric insights for comparing positive measures.
analysis.title: Optimal Entropy-Transport problems and a new Hellinger–Kantorovich distance between positive measures

content.abstract: This paper introduces PAGA (Partition-based Graph Abstraction), a novel algorithm that unifies clustering and trajectory inference for single-cell RNA-seq data. By estimating the connectivity of manifold partitions, PAGA generates interpretable, topology-preserving graph maps that reconcile discrete cell types with continuous biological processes. The method demonstrates high computational efficiency and robustness across multiple biological datasets, including hematopoiesis and embryogenesis, offering a powerful tool for analyzing complex cellular heterogeneity.

key_technical_contributions: Introduced PAGA, a method that unifies clustering and trajectory inference by estimating connectivity of manifold partitions.
Developed a topology-preserving map that generates interpretable graph-like representations of single-cell data.
Achieved higher computational efficiency for exploratory data analysis workflows.
key_scientific_conclusions: PAGA successfully reconciles discrete clustering with continuous trajectory inference.
The method preserves the global topology of data, allowing for analysis at different resolutions.
Validated the approach by inferring consistent topology across hematopoietic datasets, adult planaria, and zebrafish embryo.
Demonstrated scalability by benchmarking on one million neurons.

innovation_assessment.reason: The paper addresses a fundamental dichotomy in single-cell analysis (clustering vs. trajectory inference) by proposing a novel graph abstraction method. PAGA has become a foundational tool in the field (integrated into Scanpy), significantly improving the interpretation of complex cellular landscapes and computational efficiency.

method_strengths: Unifies two previously distinct analysis paradigms (clustering and trajectories).
Preserves global topology of the data manifold.
High computational efficiency, scalable to millions of cells.
Provides interpretable graph-like maps for exploratory analysis.
method_limitations: Relies on the quality of the initial partitioning (clustering) step.
Performance is dependent on the accuracy of the underlying KNN graph construction.
May oversimplify complex topological structures if partition resolution is not optimal.
analysis.summary: This paper introduces PAGA (Partition-based Graph Abstraction), a novel algorithm that unifies clustering and trajectory inference for single-cell RNA-seq data. By estimating the connectivity of manifold partitions, PAGA generates interpretable, topology-preserving graph maps that reconcile discrete cell types with continuous biological processes. content.abstract: This paper introduces TIGON, a dynamic, unbalanced optimal transport algorithm designed to reconstruct cellular trajectories and population growth from time-series scRNA-seq snapshots. Addressing the destructive nature of sequencing, the method utilizes a deep learning approach based on Wasserstein–Fisher–Rao distance to link unpaired data points. Validated on simulated and real datasets, TIGON demonstrates high accuracy in predicting cell transitions and growth, enabling the reconstruction of gene expression at unmeasured times and inference of gene regulatory networks.

key_technical_contributions: Development of TIGON, a dynamic, unbalanced optimal transport algorithm
Simultaneous reconstruction of dynamic trajectories and population growth from snapshots
Introduction of a dimensionless deep learning formulation to solve high-dimensional optimal transport problems
Capability to reconstruct gene expression at unmeasured time points
key_scientific_conclusions: Population growth is a critical factor for accurate temporal inference in scRNA-seq analysis
TIGON demonstrates superior robustness and accuracy in predicting cell state transitions compared to existing methods
The method successfully infers temporal gene regulatory networks and cell-cell communication

innovation_assessment.reason: The paper addresses a fundamental limitation of scRNA-seq (destructive sampling) by proposing a novel unbalanced optimal transport framework that explicitly models population growth, a factor often ignored by standard trajectory inference methods. The integration of WFR distance with deep learning for high-dimensional problems represents a significant methodological advancement published in a top-tier journal.

potential_applications: Cancer progression and tumor growth modeling

Handles unpaired snapshots from destructive sequencing
Robust to noise and high-dimensional data
Capable of inferring dynamics at unmeasured time points
method_limitations: Computational complexity associated with solving high-dimensional optimal transport
Performance likely depends on the temporal resolution and quality of input snapshots
Requires sufficient data density to accurately reconstruct continuous trajectories

content.abstract: This paper presents Monocle 2, a computational method using reversed graph embedding (RGE) and DDRTree to reconstruct complex single-cell trajectories. It introduces 'dpFeature' for unsupervised gene selection and automatically identifies branch points without prior input. Applied to myoblast differentiation, it revealed a previously unrecognized branched trajectory, demonstrating its capability to resolve complex cellular state transitions.

Introduction of 'dpFeature' for unsupervised feature selection
Application of Reversed Graph Embedding (RGE) to learn principal graphs in low-dimensional space

Monocle 2 accurately reconstructs complex trajectories with branch points
Myoblast differentiation follows a branched trajectory rather than a linear one as previously thought

innovation_assessment.reason: The paper introduces a novel algorithmic framework (RGE/DDRTree) that fundamentally improves trajectory inference by automatically resolving complex branching structures without requiring prior knowledge of cell fates, representing a significant advancement over previous linear or semi-supervised methods.

method_strengths: Unsupervised nature (no need for branch number input)
Automatic branch detection
Scalability via DDRTree
Ability to resolve complex non-linear trajectories
method_limitations: Learning cyclical or disjoint trajectories requires user parameter optimization

content.abstract: This paper introduces 'RNA velocity,' a method to predict the future state of individual cells by distinguishing between unspliced and spliced mRNAs in standard single-cell RNA-seq data. Validated in neural crest and hippocampus development, this approach transforms static snapshots into dynamic trajectories, enabling the analysis of lineage trees and transcription kinetics without metabolic labeling.

Method to predict future cell states from static snapshots
Utilization of intronic sequences (previously considered noise) in standard scRNA-seq protocols
Demonstration that common scRNA-seq protocols (SMART-seq2, 10x Genomics, etc.) capture sufficient unspliced mRNA for analysis
key_scientific_conclusions: RNA velocity can be directly estimated by distinguishing unspliced and spliced mRNAs without metabolic labeling
Standard scRNA-seq protocols contain 15-25% unspliced intronic sequences usable for velocity estimation
RNA velocity successfully reveals branching lineage trees in developing mouse hippocampus
The method predicts the future state of individual cells on a timescale of hours

innovation_assessment.reason: The paper introduces a groundbreaking concept (RNA velocity) that transforms static single-cell transcriptomic data into dynamic trajectories, solving a major limitation of the technology without requiring new experimental protocols.

potential_applications: study of transcriptional kinetics in complex tissues
method_strengths: Does not require metabolic labeling
Applicable to existing standard scRNA-seq datasets
Provides high temporal resolution (hours)
Validated across multiple technical platforms
method_limitations: Relies on the assumption of steady-state transcription kinetics
Requires sufficient sequencing depth to capture intronic reads
Accuracy depends on the correct identification and quantification of unspliced mRNA

content.abstract: This paper introduces a class of fast, parallelizable scaling algorithms to approximate unbalanced optimal transport problems. By extending entropic regularization to arbitrary positive measures, the authors generalize the Sinkhorn algorithm to allow for mass creation and destruction. The method is applied to unbalanced gradient flows and barycenters, demonstrating utility in shape modification, color transfer, and growth models.

key_technical_contributions: Extension of entropic regularization to unbalanced optimal transport problems
Generalization of the Sinkhorn algorithm for arbitrary positive measures
Development of fast, highly parallelizable algorithms operating via diagonal scaling
key_scientific_conclusions: The proposed scaling algorithms effectively solve unbalanced transport problems, unbalanced gradient flows, and compute unbalanced barycenters.
The method successfully overcomes the limitation of classical optimal transport which requires normalized probability distributions.
The approach allows for handling mass variation (creation or destruction) alongside mass transportation.

innovation_assessment.reason: The paper addresses a critical limitation of classical optimal transport (mass normalization) by generalizing the widely used Sinkhorn algorithm. This creates a unified framework for unbalanced transport, enabling new applications in fields where mass is not conserved.

method_strengths: Fast execution speed
Highly parallelizable implementation
Ability to handle arbitrary positive measures
Allows for partial displacement and mass variation
method_limitations: Provides approximate solutions rather than exact optimal transport

metadata.title: Schrödinger Bridge with Quadratic State Cost is Exactly Solvable
metadata.pdf_filename: Schrödinger Bridge with Quadratic State Cost is Exactly Solvable.pdf
metadata.apa_citation: Teter, A. M. H., Wang, W., & Halder, A. (2024). Schrödinger bridge with quadratic state cost is exactly solvable. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.00503
metadata.source_file: /mnt/e/work/CytoBridge-agent-main-rag/cytobridge_agent/cbio_agent/literature_db/literature/Schrödinger Bridge with Quadratic State Cost is Exactly Solvable.pdf

content.abstract: This paper introduces a regularized Schrödinger bridge problem incorporating a quadratic state cost-to-go, which incentivizes sample paths to remain near a nominal level. The authors successfully derive the closed-form Markov kernel for the associated reaction-diffusion PDE, proving that this regularized bridge is exactly solvable even for non-Gaussian endpoint distributions. This work generalizes existing results limited to Gaussian cases and recovers the conventional Schrödinger bridge solution in the limit of vanishing regularization.

key_technical_contributions: Proposed a regularized variant of the Schrödinger bridge with quadratic state cost-to-go
Derived the closed-form Markov kernel for the regularized Schrödinger bridge
Proved exact solvability for non-Gaussian endpoint distributions, extending beyond the Gaussian-only results in existing literature
Established connections between the new kernel and exactly solvable models in quantum mechanics
key_scientific_conclusions: The regularized Schrödinger bridge with quadratic state cost is exactly solvable
The derived solution recovers the conventional Schrödinger bridge solution as a special case when regularization vanishes
The regularization induces a state-dependent rate of killing and creation of probability mass

innovation_assessment.reason: The paper provides a significant theoretical advancement by deriving a closed-form Markov kernel for the regularized Schrödinger bridge, solving a problem previously limited to Gaussian endpoints. This extends the applicability of Schrödinger bridges to a broader class of problems in stochastic control and machine learning.

method_strengths: Exact solvability allows for precise numerical computation via dynamic Sinkhorn recursion
Generalizes solutions to non-Gaussian distributions
Theoretically rigorous derivation connecting stochastic control and quantum mechanics
method_limitations: The quadratic state cost assumption may restrict applicability in scenarios requiring other cost functions
Numerical implementation complexity for high-dimensional systems is not discussed in the abstract

content.abstract: This paper presents scMRDR, a scalable generative framework for integrating unpaired single-cell multi-omics data. It utilizes a β-VAE to disentangle representations into shared and specific components, enhanced by isometric regularization and adversarial alignment. The method outperforms existing approaches in alignment and batch correction, scales efficiently to large datasets, and supports the integration of more than two modalities.

key_technical_contributions: Proposed scMRDR, a scalable generative framework specifically designed for unpaired multi-omics integration without needing pair information or global coupling matrices.
Developed a disentanglement mechanism to separate latent representations into modality-shared and modality-specific components.
Introduced isometric regularization to preserve intra-omics biological heterogeneity.
Utilized an adversarial objective for cross-modal alignment and masked reconstruction loss to handle missing features.
key_scientific_conclusions: scMRDR achieves superior performance on benchmark datasets regarding batch correction, modality alignment, and biological signal preservation.
The framework demonstrates effective scalability to large-scale datasets.
The method successfully supports the integration of more than two omics modalities.

innovation_assessment.reason: The paper addresses critical scalability and flexibility limitations in existing unpaired data integration methods by eliminating the need for global pairwise coupling matrices and supporting more than two modalities, representing a significant methodological advancement.

potential_applications: Biological discovery from unpaired multi-omics data
method_strengths: Scalable to large-scale datasets
Flexible support for more than two omics
Does not require paired data or prior correspondences

method_limitations: Relies on the assumption that latent spaces can be effectively disentangled into shared and specific components

content.abstract: This study introduces LIGER, a computational algorithm designed to integrate diverse single-cell datasets by delineating shared and dataset-specific features of cell identity. The authors applied LIGER to human and mouse brain data, successfully integrating scRNA-seq with DNA methylation and spatial data. Key findings include the identification of sexually dimorphic gene expression, cross-species mapping of substantia nigra cell types, and the revelation of epigenomic regulation mechanisms, demonstrating the tool's utility in advancing cell type definition and disease research.

Spatial localization of fine cortical subtypes in the mouse frontal cortex
Revealed putative mechanisms of cell-type-specific epigenomic regulation

content.abstract: This review explores the integration of Trajectory Inference (TI) with Spatial Transcriptomics (ST). It argues that standard TI methods often fail on ST data due to spatial batch effects, measurement granularity, and slicing biases. The authors analyze how current state-of-the-art methods address tissue deformation and alignment, highlight remaining gaps, and identify opportunities for developing advanced spatiotemporal analysis tools.

key_technical_contributions: Systematic identification of challenges in applying Trajectory Inference to Spatial Transcriptomics data
Analysis of spatial batch effects arising from tissue deformation and slicing bias
Review of state-of-the-art Spatial Trajectory Inference (STTI) methods
Framework for understanding the impact of measurement granularity on TI
key_scientific_conclusions: Standard Trajectory Inference methods cannot be directly ported to Spatial Transcriptomics without significant modifications
Spatial batch effects introduce independent noise sources at each time point, complicating TI
Current STTI methods primarily address physical arrangement issues but often overlook measurement granularity and slicing bias
Integrating spatial and temporal dimensions requires new computational frameworks to handle tissue deformation and data discontinuity

innovation_assessment.reason: This is a review article that provides a comprehensive synthesis of the emerging field of Spatial Transcriptomics Trajectory Inference. content.abstract: STRAND is a generative model that predicts single-cell transcriptional responses to genetic perturbations by conditioning on regulatory DNA sequences rather than gene identifiers. By encoding the genomic locus sequence, STRAND parameterizes a conditional transport process from control to perturbed states. This approach enables zero-shot inference, expands genomic coverage to ~95%, and improves prediction accuracy for unseen genes and cell lines, successfully identifying locus-specific effects missed by gene-level models.

content.abstract: This seminal work solves the classical Monge-Kantorovich mass transport problem. The authors prove the existence and uniqueness of the optimal measure-preserving map for costs that are strictly convex or strictly concave functions of distance. They derive an explicit formula for this map involving the gradient of a convex potential, linking the problem to the Monge-Ampere equation and mathematical economics.

content.abstract: The paper introduces Variational Regularized Unbalanced Optimal Transport (Var-RUOT), a novel framework for recovering dynamics from sparse snapshots in high-dimensional systems like scRNA-seq. Unlike existing methods, Var-RUOT incorporates optimal necessary conditions into its network parameterization and loss function, reducing the problem to learning a single scalar field. This approach ensures solutions satisfy the principle of least action, resulting in lower action, faster convergence, and improved stability. Validated on simulated and real data, Var-RUOT also proposes a biologically aligned growth penalty function for the Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao metric.

analysis.summary: The paper introduces Variational Regularized Unbalanced Optimal Transport (Var-RUOT), a novel framework for recovering dynamics from sparse snapshots in high-dimensional systems like scRNA-seq. content.abstract: This foundational monograph by Peyré and Cuturi bridges the gap between optimal transport theory and computational practice. It details the shift from exact linear programming solvers to entropic regularization techniques, specifically highlighting the Sinkhorn algorithm. The work establishes the mathematical and algorithmic basis for using OT in machine learning, offering efficient, differentiable, and scalable solutions for comparing probability distributions.

innovation_assessment.reason: This work is a seminal monograph that synthesized the field of Computational Optimal Transport, making advanced mathematical concepts accessible to the machine learning community. It popularized the use of Sinkhorn algorithm and entropic regularization, which are now standard practice.

method_strengths: Provides a unified theoretical and algorithmic framework

content.abstract: The paper introduces SOCS, a novel optimal transport-based method for trajectory inference in time-series spatial transcriptomics. It addresses the limitation of existing methods that fail to maintain the spatial coherence of biological structures. content.full_text:
Accurate trajectory inference in time -series spatial transcriptomics with structurally -constrained optimal transport John P Bryan1,2, Samouil L Farhi2*, Brian Cleary3* 1Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA 2Spatial Technology Platform, Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, Cambridge, MA 3Faculty of Computing and Data Sciences, Boston University, Boston, MA; Department of Biology, Boston University, Boston, MA; Department of Biomedical Engineering, Boston University, Boston, MA; Program in Bioinformatics, Boston University, Boston, MA; Biological Design Center, Boston University, Boston, MA *These authors jointly supervised this work Corresponding authors : Brian Cleary , bcleary@bu.edu , Samouil L Farhi, sfarhi@broadinstitute.org Abstract New experimental and computational methods use genetic or gene expression observations with single cell resolution to study the relationship between single -cell molecular profiles and developmental trajectories. Most tissues contain spatially contiguous regions that develop as a unit, such as follicles in the ovary, or tubules and glomeruli in the kidney. We find that existing approaches designed to use ti me series spatial transcriptomics (ST) data produce biologically incoherent trajectories that fail to maintain these structural units over time. We present Spatiotemporal Optimal transport with Contiguous Structures (SOCS), an Optimal Transport -based traje ctory inference method for time- series ST that produces trajectory inferences preserving the structural integrity of contiguous biologically meaningful units, along with gene expression similarity and global geometric structure. We show that SOCS produces more plausible trajectory estimates, maintaining the spatial coherence of biological structures across time, enabling more accurate trajectory inference and biological insight than other approaches. Introduction Recent advances in single cell profiling have opened new opportunities to identify developmental trajectories and understand cellular changes underlying dynamic biological processes 1. Identifying ancestor -descendant relationships allows one to gain insight into the shifts in cell state and cell type composition, and the regulatory networks that guide development, differentiation, and activation. In general, these new technologies have opened two approaches to understand ancestor -descendant relations between cells: prospective genetic fate mappin g2–4 and computational inference based on high - dimensional single cell profiles5,6. In prospective genetic fate mapping, cells a re marked in a way that persists upon cell division ( e.g. with a transgenic fluorescent reporter or a DNA sequence barcode) such that it is possible to identify cells that share a common ancestor , as in technologies such as scGESTALT7, LINNEAEUS8, and ScarTrace9. The advantage of these techniques is that they require minimal inference or assumptions: sets of cells sharing an ancestor can be read out directly. However, with these methods it is not possible to identify and profile the ancestor cell that differentiated int o any given set of labeled descendants or to follow the trajectory .
